item.title: CVE-2026-46242 Bad Epoll, FatFs Flaws, and Avalon CrownX Malware
item.content:encoded:
New "Bad Epoll" Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Unprivileged Users Gain Root, Hits Android — Must Read

A newly disclosed Linux kernel use-after-free flaw called Bad Epoll (CVE-2026-46242) can let unprivileged users gain root on Linux systems and may affect Android, with no workaround besides applying the kernel fix. The bug is difficult but highly reliable in the published proof-of-concept, and there is no evidence yet of real-world exploitation.

  • Bad Epoll (CVE-2026-46242) is a newly disclosed Linux kernel use-after-free flaw that lets an unprivileged user gain root access on affected Linux desktops, servers, and Android systems.
  • Researcher Jaeyoung Chung found Bad Epoll, submitted it as a zero-day to Google's kernelCTF program, and built a proof-of-concept exploit that reached root about 99% of the time on tested systems.
  • The flaw can reportedly be triggered from inside Chrome's renderer sandbox and can reach Android, which the article says makes it more dangerous than many other Linux privilege bugs.
  • There is no sign Bad Epoll has been used in real attacks, and as of the article's writing it was not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
  • There is no workaround because epoll cannot be turned off, so affected users should apply upstream commit a6dc643c6931 or install their distribution's backported fix when available.

Unpatched Flaws Disclosed in Filesystem Bundled Into Millions of Embedded Devices — Should Read

runZero disclosed seven unpatched FatFs vulnerabilities affecting millions of embedded devices, where malicious USB drives, SD cards, or firmware images could cause memory corruption, code execution, crashes, or data leaks. With no upstream fixes for most flaws, vendors using FatFs must audit and patch their own firmware while users restrict physical media access and watch for updates.

  • runZero disclosed seven vulnerabilities in FatFs, a small filesystem library used to read and write FAT and exFAT formats on USB drives and SD cards.
  • The vulnerabilities can be triggered by deliberately malformed storage volumes or firmware images, and the worst cases can cause memory corruption and possible code execution on affected embedded devices.
  • runZero named affected platforms including Espressif ESP-IDF, STMicroelectronics STM32Cube, Zephyr, MicroPython, ArduPilot, RT-Thread, Mbed, Samsung TizenRT, and SWUpdate.
  • Only CVE-2026-6684, a malformed GPT partition table hang, is fixed upstream in FatFs R0.16, while runZero says there is no upstream fix for the memory-corruption bugs.
  • runZero said no attacks using these bugs had been reported as of its July 1 disclosure, but it published proof-of-concept disk images, a test harness, and a QEMU-based exploit example.

New Avalon Malware Framework Packs CrownX Ransomware Capabilities — Should Read

Researchers uncovered Avalon, a previously undocumented modular malware framework delivered through a phishing chain that can steal credentials, evade defenses, move laterally, disrupt recovery, and deploy its CrownX ransomware component. The case highlights how AI-assisted development is making complex ransomware tooling more accessible to less sophisticated attackers.

  • Cybersecurity researchers discovered a previously undocumented modular malware framework called Avalon that is distributed through a multi-stage phishing chain using a spoofed legal document email and a password-protected Proton Drive archive.
  • Avalon combines credential collection, lateral movement, remote access, recovery disruption, and ransomware execution, with its ransomware component internally named CrownX.
  • The attack chain uses an ISO image containing a document-themed Windows Shortcut that launches an MSBuild project, which loads an embedded .NET assembly and downloads a next-stage payload over HTTPS.
  • Avalon includes defense evasion capabilities aimed at reducing telemetry and hiding execution from security tools including Microsoft Defender, SentinelOne, CrowdStrike, Sophos, Elastic Endpoint, FortiEDR, ESET, McAfee, and Bitdefender.
  • Blackpoint Cyber said Avalon shows signs of AI-assisted development, while the article also describes separate research on an LLM-driven agentic ransomware infection and an AI malware that converts Telegram messages into shell commands through a public LLM API.
